body:
Political resistance and constructive work were complementary

Constructive activities were organised efforts to improve village livelihoods, public cleanliness, education and social relations. They were not simply relief work unrelated to freedom. Gandhi believed that the movement would be stronger if people reduced economic dependence, learned to cooperate across social divisions and practised service in daily life.

Non-cooperation and civil disobedience directly challenged a law, an institution or a colonial practice. Constructive work instead attempted to build useful capacities and relationships: producing cloth, creating local work, keeping common surroundings clean, removing caste exclusion, strengthening relations among religious communities and teaching children through meaningful work. The two strands could proceed alongside one another and constructive work could continue when a political campaign was suspended.

The six activities at the centre of this lesson

  • Khadi: hand-spun, hand-woven cloth associated with self-reliance and the boycott of imported textiles.
  • Other village industries: rural crafts and small-scale production that provided work and essential goods.
  • Village sanitation: clean public spaces, water sources and living conditions.
  • Removal of untouchability: ending discriminatory exclusion and supporting equal access to common facilities.
  • Communal unity: mutual respect and cooperation among religious communities.
  • Basic education: learning through productive work, connected to the child's language and surroundings.

What Gandhi's named programme tells us

Gandhi first published Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place in 1941. The expanded version has a foreword dated 13 November 1945. Its wider catalogue also included prohibition, adult education, women's concerns, health and hygiene and other work. The list was presented as illustrative rather than a closed definition. The 6 activities examined here are selected historical components, not a claim that the full programme contained only 6 items.

Khadi and village industries addressed economic self-reliance. Sanitation addressed public cleanliness. Removing untouchability addressed social exclusion. Communal unity addressed relationships among religious groups. Basic education addressed how children learned.

Prelims focus

  • Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place: first published in 1941; revised foreword dated 13 November 1945.
  • Constructive work continued alongside and between direct campaigns.
  • Khadi, village industries, sanitation, anti-untouchability, communal unity and basic education are distinct items.
  • Trap: The complete revised catalogue contained more items than the 6 treated here.

[Sources: M. K. Gandhi, Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place, "Foreword" (13 November 1945), "Introductory" and chapters 1–7, online edition consulted 21 November 2026; Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, "Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place," list of activities (consulted 21 November 2026); NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, printed pp. 119–120.]

pictures.alt: Direct action and constructive activities do different work but both support organised participation and stronger local communities.
pictures.caption: Direct protest challenged particular injustices; constructive work built the capacity for sustained participation.

title: The Constructive Programme: Strengthening Society While Resisting Colonial Rule

body:
Khadi: cloth produced through hand-spinning and hand-weaving

Khadi is cloth made from hand-spun yarn and woven by hand. The charkha spins fibre into yarn; a loom weaves yarn into cloth. Spinning and weaving are related stages, not two names for the same task. Gandhi encouraged people to spin and use khadi because hand production could provide supplementary work to rural households, keep more of the clothing process within villages and make the refusal of imported cloth practical.

Swadeshi was a wider preference for goods and productive activity connected to one's own country and community. Khadi was a particularly visible expression of swadeshi, but not every Indian-made product was khadi. Similarly, wearing khadi helped sustain local production even when the wearer was not actively taking part in a street protest.

Why other village industries formed a separate item

Village life also required goods other than cloth. Gandhi encouraged activities such as oil-pressing, hand-grinding, soap-making, handmade paper and other useful rural crafts. Their immediate purpose was to create local employment and supply ordinary needs. These industries complemented khadi, but an oil press or soap-making workshop was not a khadi unit merely because it was village-based.

Two organisations that should not be confused

OrganisationYearPrincipal field
All-India Spinners' Association (AISA)1925Hand-spinning and khadi.
All-India Village Industries Association (AIVIA)1934Rural industries other than khadi; formed at Wardha.

In Gujarat, Gandhi's Ahmedabad ashram was an important setting for experiments in spinning, weaving, manual work and self-reliant living. Thus the charkha served both an economic purpose and as a symbol of participation in the freedom struggle.

Prelims focus

  • Charkha: spinning yarn; handloom: weaving cloth.
  • Khadi: hand-spun and hand-woven cloth; associated with swadeshi and rural livelihood.
  • AISA—1925: spinning and khadi.
  • AIVIA—1934, Wardha: other village industries.
  • Trap: Oil-pressing and soap-making illustrate village industries, not khadi production.

[Sources: NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, ch. 3, "Mahatma Gandhi and Self-Sufficiency," printed pp. 31–38; M. K. Gandhi, Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place, "Khadi" and "Other Village Industries" (online edition consulted 21 November 2026); Gandhi Heritage Portal, Gandhi chronology, September 1925; Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialization, Ministry of MSME, "Genesis of MGIRI," history of AIVIA, 14 December 1934 (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Cotton is cleaned and carded, spun into yarn on a charkha, then woven on a handloom into hand-spun and hand-woven khadi cloth.
pictures.caption: The charkha produces yarn; the handloom makes cloth from that yarn.

title: Khadi and Other Village Industries: Work, Swadeshi and Self-Reliance

body:
Village sanitation: improving shared living conditions

For Gandhi, village sanitation meant making common surroundings clean and healthy. Examples included cleaning village lanes and latrines, protecting wells and tanks from pollution and keeping household waste away from water sources. These were practical actions that could reduce insanitary conditions and encourage residents and volunteers to take responsibility for shared places.

Sanitation concerned physical surroundings and public health. Gandhi also listed education in health and hygiene separately, because learning healthy habits is not identical to cleaning a village street or well. The distinction matters when an activity is matched with its immediate purpose.

Removal of untouchability: ending exclusion

Untouchability referred to caste-based practices that treated particular communities as impure and excluded them from ordinary social facilities or contact. Gandhi campaigned against such discrimination and urged people to end barriers to the use of public wells, roads, schools and temples. He also performed sanitation work himself to challenge the stigma attached to manual cleaning.

The Harijan Sevak Sangh was established in 1932 to organise work against untouchability and for the welfare of oppressed caste communities. Harijan is the historical name Gandhi used; it should be read here as part of the period's terminology, not as a required present-day label.

A distinction that appears in matching questions

Cleaning a village well is primarily a sanitation activity. Ending a caste rule that prevents people from drawing water from the well is removal of untouchability. Both might concern the same physical site, but one corrects unclean conditions and the other corrects discrimination.

Prelims focus

  • Village sanitation: clean lanes, latrines and common water sources.
  • Removal of untouchability: ending caste-based exclusion from common institutions and facilities.
  • Harijan Sevak Sangh: established in 1932.
  • Trap: Cleaning a public facility and ensuring equal caste access to it are related but distinct activities.

[Sources: M. K. Gandhi, Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place, "Removal of Untouchability," "Village Sanitation" and "Education in Health and Hygiene" (online edition consulted 21 November 2026); NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, "Nationalism in India," "The Limits of Civil Disobedience"; Gandhi Harijan Sevak Sangh, "History," establishment in September 1932 (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: The same public well illustrates sanitation through cleaning and removal of untouchability through equal access; Harijan Sevak Sangh began in 1932.
pictures.caption: Clean shared facilities and equal access to them solved different problems.

title: Village Sanitation and Removal of Untouchability: Different Forms of Social Work

body:
Communal unity: cooperation across religious differences

Communal unity meant improving relationships among India's religious communities, including Hindus, Muslims and others. Gandhi encouraged mutual respect, friendship and common public activity rather than treating one religious group as an enemy. Its immediate purpose was to overcome religious mistrust and make joint social and political action possible.

During the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation mobilisation of 1920–1921, Gandhi supported cooperation between Muslims concerned about the Khilafat issue and nationalists seeking self-government. Another simple example was his 21-day fast in 1924 in response to communal tensions. These actions were directed at relations among communities, not at producing cloth or reforming a school curriculum.

Basic education: Nai Talim and the Wardha approach

Basic Education, or Nai Talim, treated useful work as a means of learning. Instead of teaching a craft as a completely isolated subject, lessons could connect productive work to language, arithmetic, observation and knowledge of the local environment. For example, children learning to spin or weave could practise measurement and counting while also discussing the materials and their uses.

At the Wardha National Education Conference in October 1937, the scheme proposed 7 years of free and compulsory education, teaching through the mother tongue and linking education with productive manual work. These were features of the historical proposal, not a claim about a present-day school rule. This is why basic education cannot be reduced to teaching a child only one vocational skill.

Communal unity concerns relations among religious groups. Basic education concerns the way children are taught. Neither is the same as adult education, which Gandhi listed separately.

Prelims focus

  • Communal unity: religious cooperation; illustrated by the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation alliance.
  • 1924: Gandhi undertook a 21-day fast for communal harmony.
  • Wardha, October 1937: historical proposal for 7 years of free, compulsory, mother-tongue, craft-centred education.
  • Trap: Nai Talim meant education through productive work, not craft training alone.

[Sources: M. K. Gandhi, Constructive Programme: Its Meaning and Place, "Communal Unity" and "New or Basic Education" (online edition consulted 21 November 2026); NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, ch. 9, printed pp. 117–119; Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, "Chronology of Mahatma Gandhi," entry for 1924; Press Information Bureau, Government of India, feature on the Wardha Scheme of Education and the October 1937 conference (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Wardha, October 1937: 7 years of free, compulsory, mother-tongue education connected productive craft with arithmetic, language and observation.
pictures.caption: Basic education used a productive craft as a centre for connected learning.

title: Communal Unity and Basic Education: Trust Between Communities and Learning Through Work
